## In the typical poor economy, most of the income gap with the United States is a productivity gap

[0.71]{.bignum}
[The median share of an economy's gap in output per worker with the United States that is due to TFP, 143 economies, 2023]{.bignum-label}

. . .

[Not machines, not schooling: the part that capital and workers leave unexplained. Today we measure it, for any economy you choose, with the Penn World Table and a few lines of Python.]{.comment}

::: {.notes}
Open with the number, then ask: what do you think explains why Nigeria produces less than a tenth of what the United States produces per worker? Most students say capital (machines, roads) or education. The data say those matter, but the residual, total factor productivity, carries most of the gap.

The number is the notebook's own: the median TFP share of the gap in equation (8), across the 142 economies with a gap, in 2023 (0.706). It comes from Section F.10 of Appendix F.

Everything on today's charts can be redone for any economy: every chart has a menu, and the notebook has a country picker.
:::

## Three questions for today

::: {.incremental}
- **Data.** What does the Penn World Table measure, and which numbers can we compare across countries and over time?
- **Growth accounting.** How much of an economy's GDP growth came from more capital, more workers, and higher productivity?
- **Development accounting.** How much of the income gap between a poor economy and the United States is due to capital, schooling, and productivity?
:::

::: {.notes}
These are the three acts of the deck and the three branches of the mind map on the title slide: the Penn World Table and the framework (cyan), growth accounting (lavender), development accounting (green).

Both methods are accounting, not explanation. They say where the differences show up in the production function, not why an economy invested, schooled or innovated more. Chapters 5 and 6 explain the why.
:::

## Two methods, one production function

| | Growth accounting | Development accounting |
|---|---|---|
| Question | Why did *this* economy grow? | Why is *this* economy poorer? |
| Compares | one economy with its own past | economies with each other, in one year |
| Works with | growth rates of GDP, capital, labour | levels of output per worker, capital, schooling |
| Result | contributions in percentage points | shares of the gap with the United States |
| Follows | the [Growth Atlas](https://growthatlas.org/#/method) | Caunedo, [STEG Lecture 2](https://github.com/julicaunedo/STEG_Lecture2) |

[In both, total factor productivity is the **residual**: what the measured inputs leave unexplained.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
The table is Section F.1 of the appendix. Point at the last row: the growth accounting follows the method of the Growth Atlas, a study companion that decomposes GDP growth with Penn World Table 11.0; the development accounting translates Julieta Caunedo's Stata code for the STEG (Structural Transformation and Economic Growth) lectures into Python.

Our growth accounting reproduces the Growth Atlas numbers for all six default economies, 204 country-years, to within 0.012 percentage points (its rounding).
:::

# The Penn World Table and the framework {.divider background-color="#3498db"}

[Act I]{.act}

## One production function frames both methods

::: {.eqpanel}
$$Y = A\,K^{\alpha}\,L^{1-\alpha}, \qquad \alpha = 0.33$$
:::

::: {.incremental}
- $Y$ output, $K$ physical capital, $L$ labour: **measured** in national accounts
- $A$ total factor productivity (TFP): **not measured**, found as the residual
- $\alpha$ the capital share, the same everywhere: about one third (Hall and Jones 1999)
:::

[Measure what you can, and call the rest productivity.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
This is equation (1) of the appendix, the Cobb–Douglas production function of Chapters 4 to 6.

The capital share alpha = 0.33 is a classroom standard and the default of both the Growth Atlas and Caunedo's code. It is not each country's measured factor share; Section F.11 tests what happens with country labour shares.

Ask: why can't we measure A directly? Because no statistical office measures "efficiency". It is defined by the equation itself.
:::

## The Penn World Table makes output and inputs comparable across 185 economies

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
### What it provides
- GDP at **purchasing power parity**: a dollar buys the same basket everywhere
- **Capital stocks** built from past investment
- **Workers**, their **hours** and a **human capital** index from schooling
- 185 economies, 1950–2023, prices of 2021 (version 11.0)
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Two kinds of series
- **National prices** (`rgdpna`, `rnna`): growth over time, *within* an economy → growth accounting
- **PPP** (`rgdpo`, `cgdpo`, `cn`): levels *across* economies in one year → development accounting
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Feenstra, Inklaar and Timmer (2015) describe the database; it is maintained at the Groningen Growth and Development Centre.

The distinction in the right column matters and students often miss it. PWT itself recommends the national-price series to compare growth rates over time, and the PPP series to compare levels across countries. That is why the two halves of the appendix use different variables.

Section F.3 of the notebook downloads the official file (pwt110.dta, about 4 MB, from DataverseNL) and checks that the book's prepared file agrees with it: the largest relative difference in rgdpna is 4.9e-05, which is rounding.
:::

[Can we measure workers' hours and schooling for every economy, as we can measure GDP?]{.question}

::: {.notes}
Ask the room before showing the chart. Most guess that rich-country data are complete and poor-country data are patchy; the surprise is how few economies have hours before 1990.
:::

## Coverage decides which comparisons we can make

::: {.incremental}
- GDP, capital and workers: about [180]{.key} economies since 2000
- Hours: about 50 economies before 1990, mostly rich ones; [130]{.key} since 2010
- So the default labour input is **persons engaged**; hours and schooling are options
:::

[Look at your data before you analyse it: missing hours would quietly drop most poor economies.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
This is why the Growth Atlas, and our appendix, use persons engaged by default. Per-hour development accounting, as in Caunedo's code, keeps 119 economies in 2023 instead of 143.

A data-science habit to stress: always check coverage before choosing a method, because the sample can change the answer.
:::

# Growth accounting {.divider background-color="#8e44ad"}

[Act II]{.act}

## From the production function to the growth accounting equation

[Take logs, then the change from one year to the next:]{.step}

$$\ln Y_t = \ln A_t + \alpha \ln K_t + (1-\alpha)\ln L_t$$

. . .

[The change in a log is, approximately, the growth rate:]{.step}

::: {.eqpanel}
$$g_Y = \underbrace{\alpha\,g_K}_{\text{capital}} + \underbrace{(1-\alpha)\,g_L}_{\text{labour}} + \underbrace{g_A}_{\text{TFP}}$$
:::

. . .

$$g_A = g_Y - \alpha\,g_K - (1-\alpha)\,g_L \qquad \text{the Solow residual}$$

::: {.notes}
Equations (2) and (3) of the appendix. The full derivation is in Section F.4: take logs (a product becomes a sum, a power becomes a coefficient), write the same equation a year earlier, subtract, and use the approximation that a change in a log is a growth rate.

Because TFP growth is computed as the residual, the three contributions add up to GDP growth exactly, even though the log approximation is not exact. Like the Growth Atlas, we use simple yearly growth rates, 100 × (X_t/X_{t−1} − 1).

Intuition with alpha = 0.33: 3 percent more capital adds about 1 point to GDP growth; 3 percent more labour adds about 2 points.
:::

## In Python, the whole method is a `groupby` and a subtraction

```python
growth = d.groupby("iso3")[["rgdpna", "rnna", "L"]].pct_change(fill_method=None) * 100
d["gdp"] = growth["rgdpna"]
d["capital"] = alpha * growth["rnna"]                 # alpha g_K
d["labour"] = (1 - alpha) * growth["L"]               # (1 - alpha) g_L
d["tfp"] = d["gdp"] - d["capital"] - d["labour"]      # g_A, the residual
```

[`groupby("iso3")` keeps each economy's growth rates separate, so the first year of one economy is never compared with the last year of another.]{.comment}

::: {.notes}
This is the core of the notebook's growth_accounting function (Section F.5). The labour input L is persons engaged, or persons × hours, or persons × hours × the human capital index, depending on the labour argument.

The notebook first does the same thing by hand for the United States, column by column, and checks that the largest gap between the sum of contributions and GDP growth is 4e-16, zero up to rounding.
:::

## The pandemic year: what happened to U.S. productivity?

[In 2020, U.S. employment fell by about 5.5 percent and GDP by 2.2 percent.]{.question}

[Did measured TFP rise or fall in 2020? Write down your guess.]{.predict}

::: {.notes}
Collect guesses. Most students expect TFP to fall in a recession. The chart answers it on the next slide.

The numbers: GDP growth −2.16 percent; the labour contribution (1 − α) g_L was −3.67 points, so employment fell by about 5.5 percent.
:::

## In 2020, measured TFP rose: a composition effect

::: {.incremental}
- U.S. 1990–2023: GDP [2.49]{.key} percent a year = capital 0.73 + labour 0.63 + TFP 1.13 points
- 2020: labour **−3.67** points, TFP **+0.97**: employment fell much more than output, so output per remaining worker rose
- TFP swings far more from year to year than capital, which changes slowly
:::

[A one-year residual is not technology: it also absorbs who works, how hard machines run, and measurement error.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Reveal the prediction: TFP rose in 2020. Employment fell sharply while output fell much less, so the residual went up. The job losses were concentrated in lower-paid service work, so the workers who remained were, on average, more productive: a composition effect, not a burst of innovation.

The averages are printed in Section F.5 of the notebook and match the Growth Atlas (2.49, 0.73, 0.63, 1.13).
:::

## TFP explains more than half of China's growth and none of Mexico's

::: {.incremental}
- **China**: GDP 8.80 percent a year, TFP [4.92]{.key} points, capital 3.52
- **United States**: TFP 1.13 of 2.49, close to half
- **India** and **Nigeria**: large labour contributions, 1.39 and 2.18 points: fast-growing workforces
- **Mexico**: growth came from adding capital and workers; TFP [−0.11]{.key}
:::

[Investment alone did not make China grow; productivity did more than half the work.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Reveal the ranking by TFP's share of GDP growth: China 56 percent, the United States 45, India 41, Nigeria 39, Korea 37, Mexico none. The numbers are the notebook's averages for 1990–2023 with persons engaged and α = 0.33.

China's productivity growth includes the reallocation of workers from farms to factories and cities, a classic source of measured TFP in developing economies.
:::

## As economies mature, their TFP contributions shrink

::: {.incremental}
- Korea: TFP [2.88]{.key} points a year in the 1990s, [0.13]{.key} in the 2020s
- China: about 5.9 in the 1990s and 2000s, 2.5 in the 2020s
- Catch-up growth borrows ideas from the frontier: the closer to it, the less there is to borrow
:::

[Fast TFP growth is a feature of catching up, not a permanent state.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Link to Chapter 6: in the combined Solow–Romer view, economies far below the frontier can grow fast by adopting existing ideas; as they converge, growth slows toward the frontier's rate. The decade table in Section F.7 of the notebook holds the numbers.
:::

| Choice | Economy | Labour | TFP |
|---|---|:---:|:---:|
| Persons, α = 0.33 (default) | Korea | 0.95 | 1.82 |
| Total hours, α = 0.33 | Korea | [0.26]{.key} | [2.52]{.key} |
| Persons, α = 0.33 (default) | China | 0.36 | 4.92 |
| Persons, α = 0.40 | China | 0.32 | [4.21]{.key} |

[Average contributions, percentage points a year, 1990–2023.]{.step}

[Hours per Korean worker fell, so counting hours moves growth from labour to TFP; a higher α moves China's growth from TFP to capital.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
In the notebook, the Fig. 4 widget has a slider for α and a menu for the labour measure: persons engaged, total hours (emp × avh), quality-adjusted hours (emp × avh × hc).

Quality-adjusted hours move growth from TFP to labour in economies where schooling rose fast. Ask students to try Nigeria with hours: its hours data start only in 2005, so its hours-based accounting starts in 2006.
:::

## "TFP growth measures technological progress"

[TFP growth is the rate of technological progress.]{.myth}

[TFP growth is a residual. Over decades it reflects ideas, organization and reallocation; in any one year it also absorbs changes in hours, skills, capacity use, commodity prices and measurement error, as 2020 showed.]{.fact .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Solow (1957) called it technical change, and Abramovitz (1956) called the residual "a measure of our ignorance". Both views are useful: the long-run average is informative; single years are not.
:::

## Mexico's growth puzzle: lots of investment, no productivity growth

[Mexico opened to trade, stabilized prices and invested, yet TFP contributed nothing to its growth since 1990. What should policy target?]{.policy}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
### What the accounting says
- Capital 0.83 and labour 1.57 points a year: all of the 2.29 percent growth
- TFP −0.11: the same inputs did not become more productive
- So more investment alone would not have closed the gap
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
### What it leaves out
- *Why* TFP stagnated: Levy (2018) points to misallocation, as informality and tax and social insurance rules keep resources in low-productivity firms
- Whether better measurement (informal output, hours) would change the residual
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Evidence: Santiago Levy (2018), Under-Rewarded Efforts: The Elusive Quest for Prosperity in Mexico, Inter-American Development Bank, argues that the allocation of capital and labour toward small, informal, low-productivity firms explains the stagnation of Mexican productivity. This is one influential reading, not a settled consensus; others stress credit, rule of law or the China shock to Mexican manufacturing.

The accounting itself only says where the growth came from: inputs, not productivity.
:::

# Development accounting {.divider background-color="#2d8659"}

[Act III]{.act}

## Why is Nigeria so much poorer than the United States?

[Nigeria's output per worker is 8.5 percent of the U.S. level. How much of that gap is machines, how much is schooling, and how much is productivity?]{.question}

::: {.notes}
Ask students to split the gap themselves first, in three percentages. Keep their answers on the board; the next slides compute them.
:::

## Add schooling, then write capital relative to output

[Output with physical and human capital, $H = hL$, divided by workers:]{.step}

$$y = A\,k^{\alpha}\,h^{1-\alpha}$$

. . .

[Substitute $k = (K/Y)\,y$, collect $y$, and raise to $1/(1-\alpha)$:]{.step}

::: {.eqpanel}
$$y = \underbrace{A^{\frac{1}{1-\alpha}}}_{\text{TFP term}} \times \underbrace{\left(\frac{K}{Y}\right)^{\frac{\alpha}{1-\alpha}}}_{\text{capital term}} \times \underbrace{h}_{\text{human capital}}$$
:::

[Each term is then divided by its U.S. value: a ratio of 0.5 means half the U.S. level.]{.step .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Equation (5) of the appendix; the derivation is in Section F.8: write k = (K/Y) y, so y = A (K/Y)^α y^α h^(1−α); divide by y^α, so y^(1−α) = A (K/Y)^α h^(1−α); raise both sides to 1/(1−α).

h is PWT's human capital index (hc), built from years of schooling and the returns to schooling. Output per worker is rgdpo/emp, and K/Y is cn/cgdpo, both at PPPs.
:::

## Why the capital–output ratio, and not capital per worker?

::: {.incremental}
- A more productive economy produces more, saves more, and **builds more capital**: part of its high $k$ is caused by TFP
- In the Solow model, $K/Y = s/(\bar{n} + \bar{d})$ in steady state: it does **not** depend on $A$
- So the capital term measures only the capital that TFP does not explain
:::

[Credit TFP for the capital it induces, and capital for the rest.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
This is the choice of Hall and Jones (1999) and of Caunedo's code. Chapter 4's development accounting, y = A k^(1/3), credits capital for all capital. Section F.10 shows how much the choice matters: the success of the inputs doubles in the capital-per-worker form.
:::

## Splitting the gap into three shares

$$\frac{y_{US}}{y_i} = \underbrace{T_i}_{\text{TFP gap}} \times \underbrace{K_i}_{\text{capital gap}} \times \underbrace{H_i}_{\text{schooling gap}}$$

. . .

::: {.eqpanel}
$$s^{TFP}_i = \frac{T_i}{T_i + K_i H_i}$$

$$s^{K}_i = \frac{K_i}{K_i + H_i}\,(1 - s^{TFP}_i), \qquad s^{H}_i = \frac{H_i}{K_i + H_i}\,(1 - s^{TFP}_i)$$
:::

[If the TFP gap equals the gap the two inputs create together, TFP's share is one half; if it is three times as large, three quarters.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Equation (8). Each gap factor is the U.S. level divided by economy i's level. This is the split in Caunedo's code (share_due_to_TFP, then the rest divided between human and physical capital in proportion to their gap factors). The three shares add up to one; the notebook checks it (largest error 1e-16).
:::

## The method in Python: three columns and a division

```python
d["y"] = d["rgdpo"] / d["emp"]                                # output per worker
d["ky"] = (d["cn"] / d["cgdpo"]) ** (alpha / (1 - alpha))      # capital term
d["h"] = d["hc"]                                               # human capital
d["tfp"] = d["y"] / (d["ky"] * d["h"])                         # TFP term, the residual
for col in ["y", "ky", "h", "tfp"]:
    d[col + "_rel"] = d[col] / us[col]                         # United States = 1
```

[Per hour instead of per worker? Divide by `emp * avh`. That is the only change.]{.comment}

::: {.notes}
The core of dev_levels and relative_to_us in Section F.9. The notebook also drops Venezuela, whose PWT output after 2017 is not plausible because hyperinflation broke its price data, and checks that the three ratios multiply to the output ratio (equation (7)).
:::

## Capital is not the problem; productivity is

::: {.incremental}

- **TFP term**: [0.088]{.key}, so TFP accounts for 92 percent of the gap

:::

[Poor economies have little capital per worker because they produce little, not the other way round.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Reveal the prediction. Numbers from Section F.9: Nigeria's y_rel 0.085, ky_rel 1.729, h_rel 0.557, tfp_rel 0.088, share_tfp 0.916. India 0.775, China 0.761, Mexico 0.709, Korea 0.702.

:::

:::

## TFP carries most of the gap, and more so where the gap is largest

::: {.incremental}
- The 31 economies below a tenth of U.S. output per worker: TFP share [0.70 to 0.88]{.key} in most cases, median 0.81
- Richer than the United States (Ireland, Norway, Switzerland, Singapore, Qatar, Brunei): the shares measure their *lead*
- Over time the cloud drifts up: TFP explains a larger share in 2023 than in 1990
:::

[The income gaps of the poorest economies are, above all, productivity gaps.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Interquartile range of the TFP share among the 31 poorest economies: 0.705 to 0.878, median 0.809 (the notebook's 2023 data).

Data hygiene: oil economies (Qatar, Brunei, Norway) look rich partly because of resource rents, which Section F.11 removes.
:::

## The typical economy's TFP share has risen since 1970 {.live-figure}

<script src="plots/plot7.js"></script>
<div class="live-plot" data-fig="plot7"></div>

[Data: [Penn World Table 11.0](https://www.rug.nl/ggdc/productivity/pwt/) (Feenstra, Inklaar and Timmer 2015). Method: Caunedo, [STEG Lecture 2](https://github.com/julicaunedo/STEG_Lecture2). Chart inspired by the development accounting of Chapter 4 in Jones (2024), [*Macroeconomics*, 6th ed.](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324063612)]{.source-line}

::: {.notes}
How to read it: the three solid lines are the medians, across economies, of the TFP share, the physical capital share and the human capital share of the gap with the United States, each year since 1970. The dotted amber line is the TFP share of the economy in the menu (starting with Nigeria).

Do live: switch the menu to China, India, Mexico, Korea.

## Schooling has spread faster than productivity

::: {.incremental}
- Median TFP share: [0.44]{.key} in 1970 → [0.71]{.key} in 2023
- The sample grows from 107 economies in 1970 to 142 from 1990 on, but the rise continues with the sample fixed
- Human capital gaps narrowed: poor economies schooled their workers faster than they raised productivity
:::

[As schooling gaps close, what remains of the income gap is ever more a productivity gap.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Numbers: the median TFP share 0.438 in 1970, 0.551 in 1990, 0.626 in 2010, 0.706 in 2023; physical capital 0.243 → 0.110; human capital 0.309 → 0.172 (Section F.10).
:::

## Inputs explain only 16 percent of the spread of incomes

$$\text{success} = \frac{\operatorname{var}\left[\ln y^{KH}\right]}{\operatorname{var}\left[\ln y\right]}, \qquad y^{KH} = (K/Y)^{\alpha/(1-\alpha)}\,h$$

| Form of the factor-only model | Success, 143 economies, 2023 |
|---|:---:|
| capital–output form (this appendix, Caunedo) | [0.157]{.key} |
| capital-per-worker form (Chapter 4, Caselli 2005) | [0.301]{.key} |

[If every economy had U.S. TFP, the spread of log output per worker would shrink by 84 percent; how much "inputs" explain depends on who gets credit for TFP-induced capital.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Equation (9), the success measure of Caselli (2005): the share of the cross-country variance of log output per worker that a factor-only model, with the same TFP everywhere, would reproduce.

Physical capital alone 0.053, human capital alone 0.068 (the two do not add up, because they are correlated).

The success fell from about 0.21 in 1990 to 0.14 in 2010 and was 0.16 in 2023.
:::

## The result survives hours and resource rents, but not country labour shares

::: {.mid-table}
| Variant | Economies | Success of inputs | Median TFP share |
|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| per worker (baseline) | 143 | 0.157 | 0.706 |
| per hour (Caunedo) | 119 | 0.151 | 0.713 |
| net of resource rents | 140 | 0.150 | 0.734 |
| country labour shares | 119 | [1.944]{.key} | 0.846 |
:::

[A success above 1 is impossible: where the labour share is tiny (Qatar 0.18), the capital exponent $(1-0.18)/0.18 \approx 4.6$ explodes.]{.takeaway .fragment}

::: {.notes}
Section F.11. Net of rents: GDP is scaled by (1 − rents/100), with the World Bank's total natural resource rents, and Ireland and Macao are dropped, as in Caunedo's code. Labour shares: PWT's labsh, which counts resource rents and the income of the self-employed as capital income in many economies; Gollin (2002) shows that adjusting for self-employment makes labour shares much more similar across countries. That is why development accounting keeps one common α.
:::

## "Poor countries are poor because they lack machines"

[Poor countries are poor mainly because they have too little capital.]{.myth}

[Relative to their output, poor economies have as much capital as the United States: Nigeria's capital term is 1.73, India's 1.12. Capital per worker is low because output is low, and output is low mainly because TFP is low.]{.fact .fragment}

::: {.notes}
This is the central lesson of development accounting since Hall and Jones (1999) and Caselli (2005). It does not mean capital is unimportant: TFP-induced capital is real capital; the accounting credits it to TFP because TFP caused it.
:::

## If productivity is the gap, what should policy target?

[A finance ministry wants to close the gap with richer economies. Subsidize investment, expand schooling, or remove what keeps productivity low?]{.policy}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
### What the accounting suggests
- Investment alone raises $K/Y$, which is already near the U.S. level
- Schooling closes part of the gap (Nigeria's $h$ is 0.56)
- Most of the gap is TFP: how well inputs are used
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
### What it leaves out
- What TFP *is*: institutions and "social infrastructure" (Hall and Jones 1999), misallocation across firms (Hsieh and Klenow 2009), technology adoption
- Whether `hc` measures skills well: Hendricks and Schoellman (2023) find a larger role for human capital
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Hsieh and Klenow (2009) estimate that reallocating capital and labour across manufacturing plants to U.S. levels of efficiency would raise manufacturing TFP by 30–50 percent in China and 40–60 percent in India. Hall and Jones (1999) relate output per worker to institutions and government policies. Both are influential; the size of the effects is debated.

Development accounting itself prescribes nothing; it tells policymakers where the gap is.
:::

## A skeptic: "TFP is just a measure of our ignorance"

[A skeptic says: "You call the residual productivity, but it is simply everything you failed to measure. Saying it explains 70 percent of the gap says nothing."]{.objection}

. . .

[Reply: the skeptic is half right, which is the point. Abramovitz (1956) called the residual "a measure of our ignorance". Accounting shows how big that ignorance is, and robustness checks (hours, rents, schooling) show it does not go away when we measure more. That is why growth theory, from Solow to Romer, is about TFP.]{.rebuttal}

::: {.notes}
Use this to motivate Chapters 5 and 6 and the research on institutions and misallocation. The residual is large and robust; explaining it is the open question.
:::

## What to remember from this appendix

::: {.incremental}
- **I.** The Penn World Table gives comparable output and inputs for 185 economies: national-price series for growth, PPP series for levels
- **II.** Growth accounting splits GDP growth into capital, labour and TFP: since 1990, TFP did more than half of China's growth, close to half of U.S. growth, and nothing in Mexico
- **III.** Development accounting puts most of the income gap on TFP: the median TFP share is 0.71 in 2023, and inputs explain only 16 percent of the spread of incomes
- Both are **accounting**: they say where the differences are, not why
:::

::: {.notes}
One takeaway per act, in the order of the mind map's branches. Ask students which number surprised them most.
:::

Walk the three branches in a minute each: the Penn World Table and the framework (cyan, upper left), growth accounting (lavender, upper right), development accounting (green, bottom). Then the thesis on the next slide.
:::

## Measured inputs explain much of growth but little of income gaps; productivity, the residual, carries most of the difference {.closing background-color="#2d8659"}

[Open the Appendix F notebook in Colab, choose your own countries, and redo every chart]{.act}

::: {.notes}
The thesis of the appendix and of the mind map. Accounting splits output into what measured inputs explain and a residual, TFP. Since 1990, TFP explains more than half of China's growth, close to half of U.S. growth and none of Mexico's. Across 143 economies in 2023, the capital–output term is close to the U.S. level almost everywhere and schooling explains part of the gap, but TFP carries most of it. Accounting says where the differences are, not why.
:::
